items.t: Boundaries: NONE apply — a topic explainer has no geography of its own. The only places the page names are three municipalities mentioned as examples of GIS providers (Chilliwack, Abbotsford, Delta), which fall in three different board areas and none of which is this page's market.

The tools and sources the page names, as the page names them: "Chilliwack MapOnline, Abbotsford CityMap, and Delta's map" as the municipal GIS maps most relevant in this region for flood plain layers, and "BC iMap" for provincial flood data. The page does not name a specific tool for Langley, Surrey or any other municipality, does not name the ALC's ALR mapping, the Land Title Office or BC Assessment, and gives no URLs for any tool.
The page itself makes the same split for houses: GIS is a first look, title is the source of truth.

items.t: Regulator context: real estate trading services in BC are regulated by the BC Financial Services Authority (BCFSA), which states a licensed professional must give consumers information about commissions and fees, inform consumers of the duties owed to clients and non-clients, inform unrepresented consumers of the risks of dealing with a professional representing another party, and work for only the buyer or the seller in a transaction — the frame within which map findings become advice to a client.

items.t: The page names tools but gives the reader no route into any of them. It embeds no map, provides no link or instructions for opening any named tool, walks through no worked example on a real property, and covers no municipality where most of Jared's listings sit (no Langley, Surrey, South Surrey or White Rock tool is named) — a reader finishes the page knowing what GIS is, but with no route from the page into any actual map.
"Delta's map" gives a reader nothing to search with confidence.

The page never names the ALC's own ALR mapping, even though ALR boundaries are one of its headline GIS uses. It also never names the Land Title Office or BC Assessment. Those omissions are content observations from the page's text and the one provincial page opened, not findings about any tool's quality.

The four checks the page offers as its reason to exist are all parcel checks, not building checks. Whether a lot is "actually buildable," whether a property is in a flood zone, whether "part of the backyard is technically a creek setback," and whether a "big lot" is "actually mostly unbuildable" — for a condo buyer those questions attach to the land under the building and to any redevelopment argument, while price, fees and levies still turn on the strata documents.
Surface flood status before subjects, not after.

items.t: Zoning versus OCP — the page's plain-language framing only: "Zoning is the current rule — what you're allowed to build on the property today.

The verified provincial tool: iMapBC is the Province's own viewer for thousands of geographic datasets, with upload, print and email functions — the one tool named (as "BC iMap") on this page that the research could confirm against its owner's own description.

The regulator context for acting on what a map shows: real estate trading services in BC are regulated by the BC Financial Services Authority (BCFSA), which states a licensed professional must give consumers information about commissions and fees, inform consumers of the duties owed to clients and non-clients, inform unrepresented consumers of the risks of dealing with a professional representing another party, and work for only the buyer or the seller in a transaction — the frame within which map findings become advice to a client.

: Property transfer tax general tiers are 1% on the first $200,000, 2% to $2 million, 3% above $2 million, plus a further 2% on the residential portion above $3 million. Worked examples, inputs + tier math stated (fully residential, no exemption unless stated): $500,000 → $2,000 + $6,000 = $8,000; $700,000 → $2,000 + $10,000 = $12,000; $800,000 → $2,000 + $12,000 = $14,000 (fully-qualifying first-time buyer: $6,000); $1,500,000 → $2,000 + $26,000 = $28,000; $1,800,000 → $2,000 + $32,000 = $34,000; $3,500,000 → $2,000 + $36,000 + $45,000 + $10,000 (further 2% tier) = $93,000.
: A buyer checking a specific parcel works from that parcel's own municipal and provincial records, not from this explainer.

items.t: The provincial tool's real name is one word different: the page names "BC iMap" for flood data; the Province styles its own tool iMapBC — the name a buyer should search. The page also never mentions the ALC's own ALR mapping even though ALR boundaries are one of its headline GIS uses.

"Delta's map" gives a reader nothing to search with confidence: the municipal tools are named without links and without the municipalities' own product names being verifiable from the page — the names are recorded as the page's statements only, not verified as current products.
A map line is not an encumbrance record: the page is explicit that not every encumbrance shows up on a map — the absence of a line on a GIS screen proves nothing about a parcel's title.

blocks.text: Duplexes and half duplexes in Geographic Information Systems
Local rules that affect duplexes in Geographic Information Systems

items.t: "Zoning is the current rule — what you're allowed to build on the property today. OCP (Official Community Plan) is what the city wants the area to become over the next 10-30 years," with the page's worked example that a single-family-zoned property with a medium-density OCP designation "is a redevelopment opportunity." No municipal bylaw or OCP was opened to test those definitions; quote them only as the page's plain-language framing.

Flood plain checking, as the page describes the mechanics: "Most municipal GIS maps have a flood plain layer you can toggle on," the named regional tools are Chilliwack MapOnline, Abbotsford CityMap and Delta's map, BC iMap holds provincial flood data, and a flood plain location "doesn't mean you can't buy it — but insurance, lending, and rebuilding rules change." Whether any named municipal tool in fact carries a toggleable flood layer under that name today, and the flood status of any specific property: Not verified — no municipal GIS tool was opened and no property was looked up.

faq.q: How do I find out if a property is in a flood plain?

faq.a: No. The page itself warns a "big lot" can be "actually mostly unbuildable" once flood, creek setbacks and other layers are applied, and zoning/OCP designations must be verified with the municipality for the specific parcel — the explainer's shorthand settles nothing.
faq.q: The map shows a big lot — can I assume I can build a duplex on it?

faq.a: On the page's own answer: no — for a standard townhome or detached home in an established neighbourhood GIS is rarely critical, and it matters most for land, acreage, property near water or in a flood zone, and anything you plan to build on, subdivide or significantly modify.
faq.q: Do I need GIS skills to buy a house?

faq.a: In the page's plain-language framing: zoning is the current rule for what may be built on a property today, while the Official Community Plan is the municipality's long-term direction for the area over the next 10–30 years — so a property can be zoned for one use today and designated for denser use in the plan. Those are the page's simplified definitions, recorded as site copy, not as bylaw-verified definitions.
